candidates.attacker_control: The raw password is fully attacker/user controlled: the login request credentials flow into BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches (via DaoAuthenticationProvider / DelegatingPasswordEncoder) and registration/change-password values flow into encode. Only null is validated; there is no upper bound on length or byte count, and the BCRYPT_PATTERN check applies to the stored encoded value, not the raw input.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Verified there is no length check in BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode/matches, BCrypt.hashpw/checkpw, DelegatingPasswordEncoder, PasswordEncoderFactories, or PasswordEncoder; the only raw-input validation is the null check, and BCRYPT_PATTERN applies to the encoded value (60 chars). Noted that this Java implementation does NOT literally truncate (it mixes all bytes via streamtowords modulo), so an in-implementation collision of 72-byte prefixes is not demonstrable from source; the concrete defect evidenced is the missing enforcement/divergence from the bcrypt 72-byte specification and from truncating implementations, not a same-library collision. Reviewed other candidates (OAuth2/OIDC handler using request URL for server-side POST, OidcBackChannelLogoutTokenValidator NPE on missing iss, DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver redirect_uri built from request Host, AuthorizationManager null decision treated as granted) and found them either documented behavior, configuration-dependent, or lower impact.
candidates.impact: Credential validation flaw: passwords longer than bcrypt's 72-byte limit are silently accepted and handled non-spec-compliantly. In any environment where a truncating bcrypt implementation participates in verification, a supplied password that differs from the real password only after byte 72 authenticates successfully; in a pure-Spring deployment the stored hash becomes non-interoperable with other bcrypt implementations (and vice versa), which can also be abused during hash migration/verification gaps. Effectively, entropy/semantics beyond 72 bytes are undefined, weakening the guarantee that the full user password guards the account.
candidates.prerequisites: Application uses BCryptPasswordEncoder directly or through the default DelegatingPasswordEncoder/PasswordEncoderFactories (bcrypt is the default encode id) and permits passwords longer than 72 bytes. Impact materializes where credentials cross a bcrypt implementation boundary (e.g., migrated/imported hashes, another component or older/newer library verifying the same credential, or a truncating bcrypt in the authentication chain), or where the application assumes bytes beyond 72 add security.
candidates.root_cause: BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode(CharSequence) and matches(CharSequence,String) forward the raw password unconditionally to BCrypt.hashpw/BCrypt.checkpw, and the underlying BCrypt.hashpw(String,String)/hashpw(byte[],String)/hashpw(byte[],String,boolean) routines contain no check that the UTF-8 password is at most 72 bytes. bcrypt ("$2a/$2b/$2y") defines 72 bytes as the maximum effective password length and widely used implementations truncate input at that boundary. This implementation instead cycles the complete byte array through the Blowfish key schedule (streamtowords: `off = (off + 1) % data.length`), so a >72-byte password yields a hash that neither matches a spec-compliant/truncating bcrypt hash nor is truncated consistently.
candidates.title: BCryptPasswordEncoder/BCrypt do not enforce bcrypt's 72-byte maximum password length
candidates.trace: BCryptPasswordEncoder.matches (120-134) -> BCrypt.checkpw(String,String) (762-765) -> hashpwforcheck (578-580) -> hashpw(byte[],String,boolean) (606-671) -> crypt_raw/ekskey/key (no length check anywhere). BCryptPasswordEncoder.encode (104-111) -> getSalt (113-118) -> BCrypt.hashpw(String,String) (588-594) -> hashpw(byte[],String) (602-604). Source-relation index edges confirm encode->hashpw and matches->checkpw->hashpw; no symbol in these chains performs a 72-byte/bound check (grep for MAX_PASSWORD/72 in crypto returns only Blowfish constants).
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed, and no external CVE/advisory/patch data was consulted (offline review only). Whether this specific snapshot's intended benchmark vulnerability is the bcrypt maximum-length issue (e.g., CVE-2025-22228 fixed in a later 6.3.x/6.4.x release) is inferred from version metadata and the missing check; the exact upstream fix form (reject vs truncate at 72 bytes) and which authentication deployments are exploitable were not verified. Tests are excluded from the snapshot, so no test evidence corroborates the expected behavior.
candidates.weakness_type: Missing maximum-length validation for credential input (CWE-20 improper input validation / CWE-522 insufficiently protected credentials)

coverage_summary: Read the P1 relation scope (index is partial: 1,990/2,023 files indexed, 33 source files missing; syntax-level call/containment/inheritance candidates only, no control/data flow or semantic resolution) and the source scope (2,023 files, no sensitive-name/symlink/binary exclusions; src/test trees are absent from the snapshot, some src/integration-test resources remain). I inspected representative security-sensitive areas: crypto/password encoders (BCrypt, Argon2, Pbkdf2, SCrypt, DelegatingPasswordEncoder, factories), core authentication (DaoAuthenticationProvider, reactive manager), method security interceptors/AuthorizationManager, web authorization/filters/matchers/firewall, CAS redirect filters, OAuth2 client and OIDC back-channel logout configurers/handlers, ACL JDBC and LDAP encoders. Remaining 1,700+ Java files (SAML2, RSocket, messaging, taglibs, docs, most config/web internals) were not individually read; the relation index covers navigation only and omits data/control flow, so no unreported area is claimed as reviewed.
limitations: Source snapshot has no src/test files, so expected-behavior tests for BCrypt length handling could not be compared.
No build, tests, scanners, or runtime execution were performed; all conclusions are static source reading.
External CVE/advisory/patch lookups were not available; CVE/fix-version attribution is from internal knowledge and remains an inference.

The relation index is partial (33 source files missing, 25,378 unresolved calls, no data-flow/semantic resolution), so relation edges were used only as navigation and each relevant edge was re-verified in source text.

The bcrypt >72-byte behavior depends on the verifying implementation (Spring mixes all bytes; spec-compliant bcrypt truncates), so practical exploitability depends on deployment/migration details that cannot be evaluated from this source alone.

rejected_leads.lead: OIDC back-channel logout handler builds the server-side logout POST target by expanding {baseUrl}/{baseHost} from the incoming request's Host header (config/.../OidcBackChannelLogoutHandler.java computeLogoutEndpoint, lines 117-144) and sends the session cookie/CSRF headers with it - possible SSRF/session-cookie leak.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a valid IdP-signed logout token (validated in OidcBackChannelLogoutAuthenticationProvider) plus a user-configured logoutUri template using {baseUrl}/{baseHost}; the default is localhost-anchored ({baseScheme}://localhost{basePort}/logout). This is configuration-dependent intended behavior, not a clear source-level vulnerability, and the file was not recently modified (Copyright 2002-2024).

rejected_leads.lead: OidcBackChannelLogoutTokenValidator.validate dereferences logoutClaims.getIssuer() before its null check (lines 79-82), so a logout token without iss throws NPE and yields HTTP 500 rather than a 400 invalid-token response.
rejected_leads.reason: Robustness/error-handling defect only; no authentication or authorization bypass, and rejecting such tokens still occurs (via an error path).

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver.expandRedirectUri builds the redirect_uri base from UrlUtils.buildFullRequestUrl(request) (scheme/host/port from request, lines 222-252), which can be influenced by the Host/Forwarded headers - host-header injection/open-redirect risk.
rejected_leads.reason: Documented behavior with explicit guidance in the handler configurer (use fixed logoutUri/base URLs behind proxies); exploitability depends on provider-side redirect_uri validation and deployment configuration; no source-level missing check identifies it as the intended issue.

rejected_leads.lead: AuthorizationManager.verify / AuthorizationFilter / AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor treat a null AuthorizationDecision as granted (decision != null && !decision.isGranted()).
rejected_leads.reason: By-design abstention semantics for this version; all built-in managers return non-null decisions, so no attacker-controlled null path was found.

rejected_leads.lead: SQL in ACL/JDBC/UserDetails code and LDAP filter construction.
rejected_leads.reason: JdbcTemplate parameter binding and LdapEncoder escaping were verified; no injection found in inspected paths.

summary: Scope: Spring Security (spring-projects/spring-security) source snapshot at version 6.3.8-SNAPSHOT (spring-framework 6.1.17 pin, ~mid-Feb 2025), 2,023 visible files (1,752 Java). I reviewed the crypto/password-encoding stack, core authentication providers, method-security authorization, web filters/matchers/firewalls, OAuth2 client/OIDC logout configurers, ACL/JDBC and LDAP escaping. The single strongest source-evidenced candidate is in the crypto module: BCryptPasswordEncoder and BCrypt accept arbitrarily long raw passwords, although bcrypt defines a 72-byte maximum effective password length and other implementations truncate to it. The encoder/`BCrypt.hashpw`/`checkpw` code paths contain no maximum-length validation, so for passwords longer than 72 bytes the library neither rejects the input nor implements the truncation semantics assumed by the bcrypt specification, producing divergent/non-interoperable credential behavior. This matches the class of the publicly documented BCrypt maximum-password-length issue fixed in later 6.3.x/6.4.x releases (upstream later added a 72-byte maximum check such as MAX_PASSWORD_LENGTH in BCryptPasswordEncoder). No runtime/external ground truth was consulted and this remains a lead, not a confirmed exploit.
